docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
I am dedicated Certified (GISP 162370) Geospatial Data Professional with proven expertise in remote sensing, geospatial data management, and GIS application development for federal and environmental programs.

With experience at USGS EROS, NOAA NMFS, and the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality (ADEQ), I have led transformative projects applying remote sensing, machine learning, and cloud GIS to solve critical challenges in ecosystem monitoring and environmental data management.

At USGS, I advanced automated workflows for large-scale invasive species mapping across the western U.S., integrating satellite imagery with AI-based land cover models. At ADEQ, I modernized GIS and data systems for statewide environmental programs, developing spatial tools and survey applications that improved community engagement and PFAS sampling operations.

As a co-author of several peer-reviewed publications, I demonstrate a commitment to advancing geospatial research and open, reproducible science. My vision centers on democratizing access to geospatial intelligence and empowering agencies to make data-driven environmental decisions.

docs.title: Resources

A curated library of GIS & Remote Sensing data sources, tools, libraries, courses and tutorials. Compiled from study notes and saved posts, with every link pointing to the official source (data provider, documentation or course home) rather than to any social-media post.

How to use this page

  • The Data sections are tables: Data · Uses · Link · Output format.
  • The Tools, Libraries, Learning sections are annotated link lists.
  • Availability, resolution and licensing change over time — always confirm on the provider's site before using a dataset in production.

def clip_to_polygon(mosaic, transform, crs, geometry, out_path):
    """Clip an in-memory mosaic to `geometry` and write it as a compressed GeoTIFF."""
    profile = {
        "driver": "GTiff", "dtype": "float32", "count": 1,
        "height": mosaic.shape[1], "width": mosaic.shape[2],
        "crs": crs, "transform": transform, "nodata": NODATA,
        "compress": "deflate", "predictor": 3, "tiled": True,
    }
    with rasterio.MemoryFile() as memfile:
        with memfile.open(**profile) as tmp:
            tmp.write(mosaic.astype("float32"))
        with memfile.open() as tmp:
            clipped, clipped_transform = rasterio.mask.mask(
                tmp, [geometry.__geo_interface__], crop=True, nodata=NODATA
            )

    profile.update(height=clipped.shape[1], width=clipped.shape[2], transform=clipped_transform)
    with rasterio.open(out_path, "w", **profile) as dst:
        dst.write(clipped)
    return out_path

docs.title: 🏔️ Download and Clip a DEM for Any U.S. State — Open Data, No API Key¶
docs.text:
This notebook builds a clean, state-shaped Digital Elevation Model (DEM) from free, public data. It runs top-to-bottom in Google Colab with no uploads, no Google Drive and no account or API key.

Step What happens Open source / data 1 Download the state boundary U.S. Census cartographic boundaries 2 Work out which 1° DEM tiles cover the state plain Python 3 Read only the needed pixels from cloud-hosted tiles and mosaic them Copernicus GLO-30 DEM on AWS Open Data, via rasterio 4 Clip the mosaic to the exact state outline rasterio.mask 5 Derive a hillshade and map the result numpy, matplotlib

Libraries: geopandas, rasterio, numpy, matplotlib — all open source.

To change the state, edit STATE_NAME in the configuration cell and run all cells. An optional OpenTopography alternative is at the end of the notebook.

docs.title: 2. Configuration¶
docs.text:
Setting Meaning STATE_NAME Any U.S. state, DC or Puerto Rico, spelled as in the Census NAME column TARGET_MAX_PIXELS Upper bound on output size. Large states are automatically resampled to stay under it, so the notebook runs on a free Colab instance OUTPUT_DIR Local Colab folder for results (use the Files panel to download them)

The native resolution of Copernicus GLO-30 is about 30 m. Small states are processed at full resolution; large ones are averaged to a coarser grid.

docs.title: 3. Get the state boundary¶
docs.text: The Census 1:20,000,000 cartographic boundary file is small (~0.5 MB) and contains every state. We filter it by name and reproject to WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) to match the DEM tiles.

docs.title: 4. Find the DEM tiles that cover the state¶
docs.text: Copernicus DEM tiles are 1° × 1° and named after their south-west corner (e.g. N41_00_W072_00). Tiles over open ocean do not exist, so missing tiles are skipped.

docs.title: 5. Mosaic the tiles¶
docs.text:
rasterio.merge.merge reads only the pixels inside the state's bounding box. Because the tiles are cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs, GDAL fetches just those byte ranges — and, for large states, uses the built-in overviews — rather than downloading whole tiles.

The output grid size is chosen automatically so it never exceeds TARGET_MAX_PIXELS.

docs.title: 6. Clip to the state outline¶
docs.text: The mosaic is a rectangle. rasterio.mask.mask sets every pixel outside the state polygon to a nodata value and trims the array to the polygon's extent.

docs.title: 7. Inspect and visualise¶
docs.text: Elevations are metres above the EGM2008 geoid. The hillshade is computed with Matplotlib's LightSource, with the sun in the north-west at 45° altitude.

docs.title: 9. Download your results¶
docs.text: Files are in the Colab Files panel under outputs/. The cell below also zips them and offers a browser download (it does nothing outside Colab).

docs.title: 10. Optional: OpenTopography API (SRTM / NASADEM / other DEM types)¶
docs.text:
OpenTopography serves many global DEMs through a single REST endpoint. It needs a free API key, so it is optional here.

In Colab, click the 🔑 Secrets icon, add a secret named OPENTOPO_API_KEY, and enable notebook access. Then set RUN_OPENTOPOGRAPHY = True below. The key is read from the secret and is never written into the notebook.

Supported demtype values include SRTMGL1, SRTMGL3, COP30, COP90, NASADEM and AW3D30. Requests are limited by area, so use this for a state or a sub-region rather than the whole country.

def download(url, folder="data"):
    """Download `url` into `folder` (skipped if already there) and return the local path."""
    os.makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)
    path = os.path.join(folder, os.path.basename(url.split("?")[0]))
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        with requests.get(url, stream=True, timeout=120) as r:
            r.raise_for_status()
            with open(path, "wb") as f:
                for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=1 << 16):
                    f.write(chunk)
        print(f"Downloaded {path}  ({os.path.getsize(path) / 1024**2:.1f} MB)")
    else:
        print(f"Already have {path}")
    return path

def fetch_dem(bounds, out_path):
    """Mosaic Copernicus GLO-30 tiles over `bounds` (W, S, E, N) into a GeoTIFF."""
    west, south, east, north = bounds
    sources = []
    for lat in range(math.floor(south), math.ceil(north)):
        for lon in range(math.floor(west), math.ceil(east)):
            url = DEM_TILE_URL.format(ns="N" if lat >= 0 else "S", lat=abs(lat),
                                      ew="E" if lon >= 0 else "W", lon=abs(lon))
            sources.append(rasterio.open(url))
    try:
        mosaic, transform = merge(sources, bounds=bounds, nodata=-9999.0)
    finally:
        for s in sources:
            s.close()
    profile = {"driver": "GTiff", "dtype": "float32", "count": 1, "crs": "EPSG:4326",
               "height": mosaic.shape[1], "width": mosaic.shape[2], "transform": transform,
               "nodata": -9999.0, "compress": "deflate"}
    tmp = out_path + ".part"
    with rasterio.open(tmp, "w", **profile) as dst:
        dst.write(mosaic.astype("float32"))
    os.replace(tmp, out_path)
    return out_path

docs.title: 🌍 A Tour of the Python Geospatial Stack — Open Data Workflow¶
docs.text:
A guided tour of the core open-source libraries for geospatial analysis in Python. Each section introduces one library, shows when to reach for it, and runs it on real open data — U.S. Census boundaries, Copernicus elevation and NOAA/NCEP climate reanalysis. Everything is downloaded automatically: no uploads, Google Drive or API keys (Earth Engine, section 10, is the one optional exception).

# Library Role 1 shapely Geometry objects and operations 2 fiona Reading and writing vector files 3 geopandas Tabular vector analysis 4 rasterio Raster I/O 5 xarray Labelled N-dimensional arrays 6 rioxarray Geospatial rasters in xarray 7 scipy.stats Statistics and hypothesis tests 8 folium Interactive web maps 9 leafmap Rapid interactive mapping 10 earthengine-api Planetary-scale cloud analysis (optional) 11 rasterstats Zonal statistics 12 matplotlib Static plots and maps 13 plotly Interactive charts

docs.title: Which library for which job?¶
docs.text: You have... Start with Points, lines, polygons in a table geopandas (built on shapely) A GeoTIFF or other raster rasterio Multi-band, multi-date or climate data (NetCDF, Zarr) xarray + rioxarray Polygons + a raster, want per-polygon statistics rasterstats A map to share in a browser folium or leafmap Petabytes of imagery Google Earth Engine

docs.title: 1. Shapely — vector geometry¶
docs.text:
Shapely creates and manipulates planar geometric objects (points, lines, polygons) in memory, with no file I/O. It is the geometry engine underneath GeoPandas and most other libraries here.

Geometry Constructor Point Point(x, y) LineString LineString([(x, y), ...]) Polygon Polygon(shell, holes) Multi-part MultiPoint, MultiLineString, MultiPolygon Mixed GeometryCollection

docs.title: Predicates, measurements and WKT¶
docs.text: Geometries answer spatial questions (intersects, contains, within) and report measures (area, length, centroid, bounds). WKT (Well-Known Text) is the standard text serialisation.

docs.title: 2. Fiona — vector file I/O¶
docs.text:
Fiona is a Pythonic interface to GDAL/OGR for reading and writing Shapefiles, GeoJSON, GeoPackage and more. Features come back as plain dictionaries, which is handy for streaming through large files without loading everything into memory. (GeoPandas uses Fiona or its faster sibling pyogrio under the hood.)

Task Method Open for reading fiona.open(path) Inspect .crs, .driver, .schema, len(src) Write fiona.open(path, "w", driver=..., crs=..., schema=...)

docs.title: 3. GeoPandas — vector analysis on tables¶
docs.text:
GeoPandas adds a geometry column to pandas DataFrames, so you can filter, join, aggregate, reproject and map vector data with familiar pandas syntax.

Operation Method Read file gpd.read_file(path) Reproject gdf.to_crs(epsg=...) Area / length gdf.area, gdf.length Spatial join gpd.sjoin(left, right, predicate=...) Plot gdf.plot(column=...)

docs.title: Spatial join¶
docs.text: A spatial join transfers attributes between layers by location. Here, which census tract is each city centre in?

docs.title: 4. Rasterio — raster I/O¶
docs.text:
Rasterio reads and writes GeoTIFFs and other raster formats through GDAL, exposing pixel data as NumPy arrays together with their georeferencing.

Task Code Open rasterio.open(path) Read a band src.read(1) CRS, transform, bounds src.crs, src.transform, src.bounds Clip to polygons rasterio.mask.mask(src, shapes, crop=True)

First, get a real raster: a 30 m elevation model (Copernicus GLO-30, hosted as cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs on AWS Open Data) for the Fargo area. Only the requested window is read over HTTP.

docs.title: Clipping a raster with a vector mask¶
docs.text: rasterio.mask.mask keeps only the pixels inside the given shapes. The vector must be in the raster's CRS — here the dissolved Cass County boundary, reprojected to match.

docs.title: 5. Xarray — labelled N-dimensional arrays¶
docs.text:
Xarray adds named dimensions and coordinates to NumPy arrays, so you select data by meaning (sel(lat=45)) instead of by position. It is the standard tool for climate grids, satellite time series and anything stored as NetCDF or Zarr.

Concept Description DataArray One labelled N-D array Dataset A dict-like bundle of DataArrays sharing coordinates .sel() / .isel() Select by label / by position .mean(dim=...), .groupby(...) Reduce and aggregate over named dimensions

The example dataset is NCEP/NCAR reanalysis 2 m air temperature (6-hourly, 2013–2014) over North America, from xarray's open tutorial data.

docs.title: Datasets and group-by arithmetic¶
docs.text: A Dataset holds several variables on shared coordinates, and groupby aggregates by calendar components.

docs.title: 6. Rioxarray — rasters in xarray¶
docs.text:
Rioxarray adds a .rio accessor to xarray objects for georeferencing: CRS, transform, reprojection and clipping. It connects Rasterio's file handling with xarray's labelled arrays.

.rio method Purpose .crs, .bounds(), .shape Inspect georeferencing .write_crs("EPSG:...") Attach a CRS .reproject("EPSG:...") Warp to another CRS .clip(geometries, crs) Clip to polygons

docs.title: 7. SciPy stats — statistics for spatial data¶
docs.text:
scipy.stats provides descriptive statistics, probability distributions and hypothesis tests.

Function Purpose stats.describe(data) Summary statistics stats.ttest_ind(a, b) Do two samples have different means? stats.pearsonr(x, y) Linear correlation and p-value stats.norm.fit(data) Fit a distribution

The samples below come from the real temperature series above.

docs.title: 8. Folium — interactive web maps¶
docs.text:
Folium generates interactive Leaflet.js maps from Python — no JavaScript needed. The result is a standalone HTML file.

Element Code Base map folium.Map(location, zoom_start, tiles) Marker folium.Marker(location, popup, tooltip) Vector layer folium.GeoJson(gdf, tooltip=...)

docs.title: 9. Leafmap — rapid interactive mapping¶
docs.text: Leafmap wraps several mapping backends behind one short API: basemaps, vector and raster layers, legends and split maps in a line or two. The foliumap backend used here needs no notebook widgets, so it works in Colab, Jupyter and exported HTML alike.

docs.title: 10. Google Earth Engine — planetary-scale analysis (optional)¶
docs.text:
Earth Engine runs computation server-side on Google's infrastructure, so you can process decades of global imagery without downloading it. It needs a free Google Cloud project registered for Earth Engine (non-commercial use is free).

To try it: register a project at https://code.earthengine.google.com/register, set RUN_EARTH_ENGINE = True, and put the project ID in EE_PROJECT (or store it as a Colab secret named EE_PROJECT). The first run opens a Google sign-in prompt. By default this cell does nothing, so the rest of the notebook runs without an account.

Step Code Authenticate (once per session) ee.Authenticate() Initialise ee.Initialize(project=...) Load a collection ee.ImageCollection("LANDSAT/LC08/C02/T1_L2") Pull a number back to Python .getInfo()

docs.title: 11. Rasterstats — zonal statistics¶
docs.text:
Rasterstats summarises the raster pixels that fall inside each vector polygon — mean, min, max, count, and so on. This is the core of "average elevation per tract" or "total rainfall per watershed".

Below: mean, minimum, maximum and relief of elevation for every Cass County census tract, using the DEM from section 4.

docs.title: 12. Matplotlib — static visualisation¶
docs.text:
Matplotlib is the foundation of Python plotting. GeoPandas, xarray and rasterio all draw through it, so its figure/axes model applies everywhere.

Plot Function Line ax.plot(x, y) Histogram ax.hist(data) Scatter ax.scatter(x, y) Raster / array ax.imshow(array)

docs.title: 13. Plotly — interactive charts¶
docs.text: Plotly makes charts you can hover, zoom and filter in the browser. plotly.express builds most chart types from a DataFrame in one call.

docs.text:

  • Elevation — Copernicus DEM GLO-30, © DLR e.V. 2010–2014 and © Airbus Defence and Space GmbH 2014–2018, provided under COPERNICUS by the European Union and ESA; AWS Open Data.

def fetch_dem(bounds, out_path):
    """Mosaic Copernicus GLO-30 tiles over `bounds` (W, S, E, N, EPSG:4326) into a GeoTIFF."""
    west, south, east, north = bounds
    sources = []
    for lat in range(math.floor(south), math.ceil(north)):
        for lon in range(math.floor(west), math.ceil(east)):
            url = DEM_TILE_URL.format(ns="N" if lat >= 0 else "S", lat=abs(lat),
                                      ew="E" if lon >= 0 else "W", lon=abs(lon))
            try:
                sources.append(rasterio.open(url))
            except rasterio.errors.RasterioIOError:
                pass                                  # no tile over open ocean
    try:
        mosaic, transform = merge(sources, bounds=bounds, nodata=-9999.0)   # pad, not 0, at the edges
        profile = {"driver": "GTiff", "dtype": "float32", "count": 1, "crs": "EPSG:4326",
                   "height": mosaic.shape[1], "width": mosaic.shape[2], "transform": transform,
                   "nodata": -9999.0, "compress": "deflate", "predictor": 3}
    finally:
        for s in sources:
            s.close()

    tmp_path = out_path + ".part"                     # write-then-rename: an interrupted run
    with rasterio.open(tmp_path, "w", **profile) as dst:   # never leaves a truncated file behind
        dst.write(mosaic.astype("float32"))
    os.replace(tmp_path, out_path)
    return out_path

def select_scenes(bounds, area, dates, max_cloud, target=0.98, max_scenes=3):
    """Greedily choose low-cloud Sentinel-2 L2A scenes that together cover `area`."""
    response = requests.post(STAC_URL, timeout=60, json={
        "collections": ["sentinel-2-l2a"],
        "bbox": list(bounds),
        "datetime": dates,
        "query": {"eo:cloud_cover": {"lt": max_cloud}},
        "sortby": [{"field": "properties.eo:cloud_cover", "direction": "asc"}],
        "limit": 100,
    })
    response.raise_for_status()
    items = response.json()["features"]
    print(f"{len(items)} candidate scene(s) with < {max_cloud}% cloud")
    if not items:
        raise RuntimeError("No scenes found; widen the dates or raise MAX_CLOUD.")

    chosen, covered = [], shape({"type": "GeometryCollection", "geometries": []})
    epsg = None
    for _ in range(max_scenes):
        # scenes must share one UTM zone so their pixel grids line up
        pool = [i for i in items if i not in chosen and epsg in (None, i["properties"]["proj:epsg"])]
        gains = [(round(shape(i["geometry"]).intersection(area).difference(covered).area / area.area, 2), -k, i)
                 for k, i in enumerate(pool)]            # -k keeps the least-cloudy on ties
        if not gains:
            break
        gain, _, best = max(gains, key=lambda g: g[:2])
        if gain <= 0:
            break
        chosen.append(best)
        epsg = best["properties"]["proj:epsg"]
        covered = covered.union(shape(best["geometry"]))
        if covered.intersection(area).area / area.area >= target:
            break

    coverage = covered.intersection(area).area / area.area
    return chosen, coverage

def read_reflectance(items, asset_key, bounds):
    """Mosaic one Sentinel-2 asset from `items` over `bounds` (EPSG:4326).

    Returns surface reflectance (0-1, NaN where no data), the affine transform and the CRS.
    """
    grid = None
    out = None
    for item in items:
        asset = item["assets"][asset_key]
        info = asset.get("raster:bands", [{}])[0]
        scale = info.get("scale", 0.0001)           # DN -> reflectance
        offset = info.get("offset", -0.1)           # processing baseline >= 04.00 adds +1000 to DN
        nodata = info.get("nodata", 0)

        with rasterio.open(asset["href"]) as src:
            if grid is None:                         # first scene defines the output grid
                left, bottom, right, top = transform_bounds("EPSG:4326", src.crs, *bounds)
                res = src.res[0]
                x0 = src.transform.c + math.floor((left - src.transform.c) / res) * res
                y0 = src.transform.f - math.floor((src.transform.f - top) / res) * res
                width = math.ceil((right - x0) / res)
                height = math.ceil((y0 - bottom) / res)
                grid = (x0, y0, res, width, height, src.crs)
                out = np.full((height, width), np.nan, dtype="float32")

            x0, y0, res, width, height, crs = grid
            col_off = round((x0 - src.transform.c) / res)
            row_off = round((src.transform.f - y0) / res)
            want = Window(col_off, row_off, width, height)
            have = want.intersection(Window(0, 0, src.width, src.height)) if (
                col_off < src.width and row_off < src.height and col_off + width > 0 and row_off + height > 0
            ) else None
            if have is None:
                continue
            dn = src.read(1, window=have)

        values = dn.astype("float32") * scale + offset
        values[dn == nodata] = np.nan
        r0, c0 = int(have.row_off - row_off), int(have.col_off - col_off)
        target = out[r0:r0 + dn.shape[0], c0:c0 + dn.shape[1]]
        gaps = np.isnan(target)                     # earlier scenes win; later ones fill the gaps
        target[gaps] = values[gaps]

    transform = rasterio.transform.from_origin(x0, y0, res, res)
    return out, transform, crs

def calculate_geomorphology(dem, cell_size, azimuth=AZIMUTH, zenith=ZENITH):
    """Return slope (deg), aspect (deg) and hillshade (0-255) for a DEM in metres."""
    dz_drow, dz_dcol = np.gradient(dem, cell_size)       # rows run north -> south

    slope_rad = np.arctan(np.hypot(dz_dcol, dz_drow))
    slope = np.degrees(slope_rad)

    aspect_rad = np.arctan2(-dz_dcol, dz_drow)           # direction the slope faces
    aspect = np.degrees(aspect_rad) % 360

    az, zen = np.radians(azimuth), np.radians(zenith)
    hillshade = 255 * (np.cos(zen) * np.cos(slope_rad)
                       + np.sin(zen) * np.sin(slope_rad) * np.cos(az - aspect_rad))
    return slope, aspect, np.clip(hillshade, 0, 255)

docs.title: 🛰️ Raster Data Processing with Rasterio — Open Data Workflow¶
docs.text:
A complete raster workflow on a real area — Billings County, North Dakota (home of Theodore Roosevelt National Park's badlands) — built entirely from free, keyless sources:

Data Source Elevation (30 m DEM) Copernicus GLO-30 on AWS Open Data County boundary U.S. Census TIGER/Line tracts Optical imagery (NIR, SWIR) Sentinel-2 L2A cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs via the Earth Search STAC API

No uploads, Google Drive or API keys. To analyse another county, change COUNTY_FIPS in the configuration cell.

# Topic 1 Acquiring and inspecting a DEM 2 Reprojecting a raster 3 Visualising and analysing elevation 4 Writing GeoTIFFs 5 Clipping with a vector boundary 6 Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) from Sentinel-2 7 Overlaying raster and vector layers 8 Slope, aspect and hillshade

Libraries: rasterio, geopandas, numpy, matplotlib, requests, shapely

docs.title: County boundary¶
docs.text: Tracts are dissolved into a single county polygon. It is used to define the study area, to download only what is needed, and to clip results.

docs.title: 1. Acquiring and inspecting a DEM¶
docs.text: Copernicus GLO-30 is distributed as 1° × 1° cloud-optimised GeoTIFF tiles named after their south-west corner. The helper below finds the tiles that cover the study area and mosaics only the pixels inside its bounding box — GDAL fetches just those byte ranges over HTTP, so nothing large is downloaded.

docs.title: Metadata¶
docs.text:
A raster file stores a grid of values plus the metadata that places it on Earth.

Property Meaning crs Coordinate reference system res Pixel size in CRS units transform Affine matrix mapping pixel (row, col) to map coordinates nodata Value that marks "no data" bounds Extent in CRS units

docs.title: Resolution in degrees vs. metres¶
docs.text: A geographic CRS (WGS 84) stores pixel size in decimal degrees, and a degree of longitude shrinks with latitude. Multiplying by about 111,320 m/° gives a rough size; reprojecting to a metric CRS gives exact metres.

docs.title: 2. Reprojecting a raster¶
docs.text: Reprojection transforms a raster to a new CRS. calculate_default_transform works out the output grid, and reproject resamples the pixels. Bilinear resampling suits continuous data such as elevation; use nearest for categorical rasters such as land cover.

docs.title: 4. Writing processed rasters to GeoTIFF¶
docs.text: To save a NumPy array as a georeferenced raster, copy the source profile (CRS, transform, size, ...) and update only the fields that changed — here the band count, data type, compression and nodata value.

docs.title: 5. Clipping a raster with a vector boundary¶
docs.text:
Clipping keeps only the raster cells inside a polygon. The vector and raster must share a CRS — reproject the vector to match the raster, never the other way around.

Step Code Load and align vector gdf.to_crs(src.crs) Clip rasterio.mask.mask(src, shapes, crop=True, nodata=...) Update profile new height, width, transform

docs.title: 6. Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) from Sentinel-2¶
docs.text:
$$\text{NBR} = \frac{\text{NIR} - \text{SWIR2}}{\text{NIR} + \text{SWIR2}}$$

Healthy vegetation reflects strongly in the near-infrared and absorbs shortwave infrared, so NBR is high (towards +1). Burned or bare ground flips this, giving low or negative values. Fire severity is normally measured as dNBR — the difference between pre- and post-fire NBR. The single-date map below shows vegetation condition and demonstrates the workflow.

Getting the imagery. The Earth Search STAC API catalogues Sentinel-2 L2A (surface reflectance) scenes stored as cloud-optimised GeoTIFFs on AWS. A county rarely fits inside one 110 km scene, so we search for low-cloud summer scenes and greedily pick up to three that together cover the county, then read only the pixels inside it. Bands used: nir08 (B8A, 865 nm) and swir22 (B12, 2190 nm), both at 20 m.

docs.title: Clip NBR to the county and visualise¶
docs.text: The Sentinel-2 grid is in a UTM zone, so the county polygon is reprojected to match before clipping. A diverging colormap centred on zero suits an index that runs from −1 to +1.

docs.title: Classifying NBR¶
docs.text: Thresholds follow the commonly used USGS dNBR severity table. Applied to a single-date NBR they are only a demonstration of reclassifying a raster with np.digitize.

docs.title: 7. Overlaying raster and vector data¶
docs.text: Plotting vectors over a raster gives spatial context. As always, both layers must share a CRS; convert the vector, not the raster.

docs.title: 8. Terrain derivatives: slope, aspect and hillshade¶
docs.text:
Derived products reveal terrain beyond raw elevation.

Product Meaning Unit Slope Steepness degrees (0–90) Aspect Compass direction the slope faces degrees (0 = north, clockwise) Hillshade Simulated illumination from a light source 0–255

All three come from the DEM's gradient. They must be computed on a projected DEM so that horizontal and vertical units agree (both metres).

docs.title: Data credits and next steps¶
docs.text:
• Copernicus DEM GLO-30 — © DLR e.V. 2010–2014 and © Airbus Defence and Space GmbH 2014–2018, provided under COPERNICUS by the European Union and ESA. Free use under the Copernicus DEM licence; hosted on the AWS Open Data Registry.
  • Sentinel-2 L2A — contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data, via Element 84 Earth Search.
  • Boundaries — U.S. Census Bureau TIGER/Line (public domain).

Next: multi-date dNBR for real burn severity, other spectral indices (NDVI, NDWI), zonal statistics with rasterstats, and time-series analysis with xarray and stackstac.

import os

def download(url, folder="data"):
    """Download `url` into `folder` (skipped if already there) and return the local path."""
    os.makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)
    path = os.path.join(folder, os.path.basename(url.split("?")[0]))
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        with requests.get(url, stream=True, timeout=120) as r:
            r.raise_for_status()
            with open(path, "wb") as f:
                for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=1 << 16):
                    f.write(chunk)
        print(f"Downloaded {path}  ({os.path.getsize(path) / 1024**2:.1f} MB)")
    else:
        print(f"Already have {path}")
    return path

docs.title: 🗺️ Vector Data Processing with GeoPandas — Open Data Workflow¶
docs.text:
A hands-on tour of vector GIS in Python, using U.S. Census TIGER/Line boundaries for North Dakota and, optionally, American Community Survey (ACS) data. Boundaries download automatically from free public sources — no uploads, Google Drive or API keys. Only the optional ACS sections (9–10) need a free Census API key.

# Topic 1 Reading vector data (Shapefile, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, URLs) 2 Inspecting a GeoDataFrame 3 Filtering and subsetting 4 Reprojecting for accurate measurements 5 Area, centroid, buffer, hull, geometry validation 6 Static maps and choropleths 7 Small-multiple county maps 8 Exporting to common formats 9 Optional: Census ACS data via the Census API 10 Joining attributes and mapping them 11 Dissolve and spatial join

Libraries: geopandas, shapely, matplotlib, numpy, pandas, mapclassify

docs.title: 1. Reading vector data¶
docs.text: gpd.read_file() detects the format automatically and returns a GeoDataFrame: a pandas DataFrame with a special geometry column. It reads zipped shapefiles directly, so there is no need to unzip anything.

docs.title: Other formats, and reading straight from a URL¶
docs.text: The same function reads GeoJSON, GeoPackage, GeoParquet and more. It can also read a remote file directly. Below, the Census state boundaries are read from a URL, then written to and re-read from GeoJSON and GeoPackage.

docs.title: Building a GeoDataFrame from scratch¶
docs.text: Any table with coordinates can become a GeoDataFrame. Populations are approximate.

docs.title: 2. Exploring a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text: A GeoDataFrame has every pandas method plus spatial properties: .crs, .geom_type, .total_bounds, .area, and so on.

docs.title: 3. Filtering and subsetting¶
docs.text: Boolean indexing works exactly as in pandas. Cass County (Fargo) has FIPS code 017.

docs.title: 4. Reprojecting for accurate measurements¶
docs.text: Geographic coordinates (degrees) are fine for storage but not for measuring: one degree of longitude is a different distance at every latitude. Reproject to a projected CRS in metres before computing area, length or buffers. EPSG:5070 (CONUS Albers Equal Area) preserves area across the contiguous U.S.

docs.title: 5. Spatial operations¶
docs.text: Shapely geometry methods are available on the whole geometry column at once.

docs.title: Validating geometries¶
docs.text: Invalid geometries (self-intersections, for example) break overlay operations. Check first; buffer(0) or shapely.make_valid repairs most problems.

docs.title: 6. Visualising with Matplotlib¶
docs.text: gdf.plot() wraps Matplotlib, so every Matplotlib option applies. Passing column= makes a choropleth.

docs.title: 7. Small-multiple county maps¶
docs.text: Loops plus plt.subplots() generate many comparable maps automatically.

docs.title: 8. Exporting results¶
docs.text: Format Best for Caveat Shapefile Legacy GIS software 10-character column names, 2 GB limit GeoPackage Modern, single-file exchange — GeoJSON Web mapping Always WGS 84 by convention; large files GeoParquet Big data, fast I/O Needs pyarrow CSV + WKT Spreadsheets Loses CRS information

docs.title: 9. Optional: Census demographic data (free API key)¶
docs.text:
Boundaries are open and keyless, but the Census Bureau's data API now requires a free key. Request one here (it arrives by email in a minute).

In Colab, click the 🔑 Secrets icon, add a secret named CENSUS_API_KEY, and enable notebook access. Locally, set an environment variable of the same name. If no key is found, this section and the next are skipped and the rest of the notebook is unaffected.

Variables used (ACS 2021 5-year Data Profiles):

Code Meaning DP02_0067PE % of population 25+ with a high-school diploma or higher DP02_0152PE % of households with a computer and broadband internet DP03_0062E Median household income ($) DP05_0001E Total population

docs.title: 10. Join attributes and map them¶
docs.text: Tables join to geometry through a shared key. For census tracts that key is GEOID. The ACS 2021 estimates use 2020-census tract boundaries, which match TIGER 2025 for most but not all tracts, so an inner join may drop a few.

docs.title: 11. Dissolve and spatial join¶
docs.text:
• Dissolve merges features that share an attribute value (tracts → counties) and aggregates their columns.
  • Spatial join transfers attributes between layers based on a spatial relationship (here: which tract does each point fall inside?).

docs.title: Data credits and next steps¶
docs.text:
• Boundaries — U.S. Census Bureau TIGER/Line and cartographic boundary files (public domain).
  • Attributes (optional) — U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2021 5-year estimates.

Next: web maps with folium and leafmap, spatial indexing with geopandas.sindex, overlay with gpd.overlay, and network analysis with osmnx.

def ensure(*specs):
    """pip-install any package that cannot be imported.

        try:

        except ImportError:
            subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", pip_name])

OSRM_URL = "https://router.project-osrm.org/route/v1/driving/{lon1},{lat1};{lon2},{lat2}"


def get_routes(origin, destination, alternatives=False):
    """Return the list of OSRM routes between two (lat, lon) points."""
    url = OSRM_URL.format(lon1=origin[1], lat1=origin[0], lon2=destination[1], lat2=destination[0])
    response = requests.get(
        url,
        params={"overview": "full", "geometries": "geojson",
                "alternatives": str(alternatives).lower()},
        timeout=60,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    data = response.json()
    if data.get("code") != "Ok":
        raise RuntimeError(f"Routing failed: {data.get('code')} {data.get('message', '')}")
    return data["routes"]

docs.title: 🌐 Interactive Web Maps with Folium — Open Data Workflow¶
docs.text:
Folium turns Python data into interactive Leaflet maps. This notebook builds up from a blank basemap to a multi-layer map of North Dakota with counties, roads and a driving route. All data comes from free public services — no API keys, uploads or Google Drive:

Source Used for OpenStreetMap / CARTO Basemap tiles OSRM public demo server Driving routes (keyless; please keep requests light) U.S. Census TIGER/Line via pygris County boundaries and roads # Topic 1 Basic maps and basemaps 2 Markers, popups, tooltips, circles 3 Custom icons and HTML labels 4 Routing with OSRM 5 Parsing GeoJSON and comparing routes 6 Saving maps as standalone HTML 7 Downloading Census data with pygris 8 GeoDataFrame.explore() 9 Categorising and styling roads 10 Layer control and basemap switching 11 Shapes, heatmaps and marker clusters

docs.title: 1. Basic maps¶
docs.text:
folium.Map() needs a centre (location=[lat, lon]) and a starting zoom. In a notebook, the last expression in a cell — here m — is rendered as an interactive map.

Leaflet and Folium use latitude, longitude order; GeoJSON and most GIS tools use longitude, latitude. Mixing them up is the most common mapping bug.

docs.title: Basemaps¶
docs.text: The tiles argument selects the basemap. Light, low-contrast basemaps such as CartoDB positron keep attention on your data.

docs.title: 2. Markers, popups and circles¶
docs.text:
• Popup — rich HTML shown on click.
  • Tooltip — text shown on hover.
  • Circle — radius in metres, so it scales with the map (good for buffers).
  • CircleMarker — radius in pixels, so it keeps its size when you zoom.

docs.title: 3. Custom icons¶
docs.text: folium.Icon changes a marker's colour and glyph (Bootstrap or Font Awesome). DivIcon places arbitrary HTML on the map, which is handy for text labels.

docs.title: 4. Routing with OSRM¶
docs.text:
The Open Source Routing Machine offers a free public demo server for driving directions — no key required. It is meant for light, non-commercial use; for production, run your own OSRM/Valhalla instance or use a hosted service.

The URL pattern is /route/v1/driving/{lon1},{lat1};{lon2},{lat2}. Note the longitude-first order. With geometries=geojson the route comes back as a GeoJSON line that Folium can draw directly, and alternatives=true asks for alternative routes where they exist.

docs.title: 5. Parsing the response and drawing the route¶
docs.text: Each route carries distance (metres), duration (seconds) and a GeoJSON geometry.

docs.title: Comparing alternative routes¶
docs.text: Request alternatives for a shorter trip and draw each one in its own colour, with a layer control to toggle them.

docs.title: 6. Saving maps as standalone HTML¶
docs.text: A Folium map is just an HTML file with embedded JavaScript, so anyone can open it in a browser — no Python needed.

docs.title: 7. Downloading Census geography with pygris¶
docs.text: pygris downloads TIGER/Line geographies straight into GeoDataFrames — no manual download or unzipping.

docs.title: 8. Multi-layer maps with .explore()¶
docs.text: GeoDataFrame.explore() builds a Folium layer from a GeoDataFrame in one call. Pass an existing map with m= to stack layers. column= makes a choropleth (this needs mapclassify, installed above).

docs.title: 9. Categorising and styling roads¶
docs.text: TIGER road features have an RTTYP route-type code: I Interstate, U U.S., S State, C County, M common name, O other. We map those codes to readable categories.

docs.title: 10. Layer control and basemap switching¶
docs.text: folium.LayerControl() adds a toggle widget. Extra TileLayers become selectable basemaps. Add the control last, after every layer.

docs.title: 11. Shapes, heatmaps and marker clusters¶
docs.text: The heatmap and cluster examples use synthetic random points inside North Dakota's bounding box purely to demonstrate the plugins.

docs.title: Data credits and next steps¶
docs.text:
• Basemaps — © OpenStreetMap contributors; © CARTO.
  • Routing — OSRM public demo server, using OpenStreetMap data.
  • Boundaries and roads — U.S. Census Bureau TIGER/Line (public domain).

Go further with leafmap for raster layers and split maps, geemap for Earth Engine, and folium.plugins for drawing tools, time sliders and minimaps.

docs.title: Nepal Hydro-Climatic Risk Atlas
docs.text:
An integrated decision-support system for flood and groundwater risk assessment.

Live dashboard Source code

Google Earth Engine scikit-learn SHAP Streamlit GeoPandas Folium

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Nepal faces a hydrological paradox: the same municipal units often suffer floods in the monsoon and groundwater depletion in the dry season. This project builds a single Compound Risk Index that highlights where both hazards overlap, and serves it through an interactive dashboard so planners can prioritise interventions such as Managed Aquifer Recharge.

The pipeline was first built for Saptari district and then generalised into a repeatable, per-district workflow. It currently scores municipal units in 45 of Nepal's 77 districts and can be extended to the rest.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
1. Data acquisition (Google Earth Engine) — 2019–2025 time series per block from CHIRPS rainfall, MODIS evapotranspiration and Sentinel-2 NDVI.
  2. Flood pressure model — Random Forest regressor (R² > 0.85) driven by 3-month cumulative rainfall, rainfall anomaly against the 30-year mean, and NDVI.
  3. Groundwater stress model — Random Forest regressor driven by evapotranspiration, rainfall and their ratio.
  4. Explainable AI — SHAP shows why a block scores high. It reveals a tipping point: groundwater stress rises sharply once the ET-to-rainfall ratio exceeds about 7.
  5. Compound score — both indices are min-max normalised and averaged 50/50; the top 20 % of blocks are classed as Critical.
  6. Trend analysis — an OLS slope over 2019–2025 gives each block a degradation rate (rising stress) or recovery rate (falling stress).
  7. Web app — a Streamlit dashboard with maps, filters and trend metrics.

docs.text:
• Three step-by-step notebooks: boundary preparation, GEE extraction, and feature merging / modelling / final outputs.
  • Command-line scripts to extract, score and publish any district.
  • TUTORIAL.md — an end-to-end guide from GEE extraction to Streamlit Cloud deployment.
